analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes farm subsidies, conservation, rural development, and food stamp programs through 2007.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 291-120 and the Senate 58-40, the conference report cleared both chambers, and the President signed it on May 13, 2002 as Public Law 107-171.
analysis.plain_summary: This farm bill locks in five more years of payments to growers of wheat, corn, cotton, rice, soybeans and other program crops, extends price supports for sugar and dairy, buys out the old peanut quota system, and renews conservation, rural development, trade, and food stamp programs through 2007 [S5]. It also restores some food stamp eligibility for legal immigrants and raises the standard deduction for low-income households [S5]. The largest and most reliable stream of money goes to commodity, sugar, dairy, and peanut interests, funded by taxpayers and, for sugar and dairy, by consumers through higher prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Producers of program commodities receive guaranteed direct payments every year through 2007 whether prices are high or low, plus counter-cyclical payments whenever prices fall below target levels and marketing loans that cushion low prices [S5]. Sugar and dairy operations get continued price support and loan programs, and peanut quota holders receive compensation for the loss of their quota asset [S5]. Low-income households gain from a higher food stamp standard deduction, transitional benefits for families leaving welfare, and restored eligibility for legal immigrant children and long-term residents [S5]. Beginning farmers get expanded credit programs, and rural communities get broadband, water, and renewable-energy funding [S5].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Commodity, sugar, dairy and peanut producers

how_it_helps.text: The food stamp standard deduction is set at 8.31 percent of the federal poverty guideline, and states may give up to five months of transitional food stamps to families leaving welfare [S5].
Legal immigrant children become eligible for food stamps and SSI regardless of entry date, and legal immigrants who have resided in the U.S. for five years regain food stamp eligibility [S5].

The bill creates a Conservation Security Program and extends and enlarges the Conservation Reserve, Wetlands Reserve, and Environmental Quality Incentives programs, which pay landowners to protect soil, water, and habitat [S5].
Rural communities gain loan authority for broadband service, expanded water and wastewater grants, and loans and grants for on-farm renewable energy systems and energy efficiency [S5].
Retailers must label the country of origin for beef, pork, lamb, fish, peanuts, and fresh produce, and the bill extends family-farmer bankruptcy protections for seven months [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the direct and counter-cyclical payments, marketing loans, peanut quota buyout, conservation, and rural programs through the Commodity Credit Corporation [S5]. Consumers pay more for sugar and dairy products because price supports and marketing allotments keep domestic prices above what an open market would produce, and food manufacturers pass those costs on [S5]. Because direct payments are tied to historical base acres rather than current need, the benefits concentrate on operations with large acreage bases.

drawbacks.text: The Senate-passed bill capped direct and counter-cyclical payments at $75,000 per person and barred payments to anyone with adjusted gross income above $2.5 million [S4]. The House voted 265-158 to instruct its conferees to adopt those tighter limits [S12], but the final bill instead allows $40,000 in direct payments, $65,000 in counter-cyclical payments, and $75,000 in marketing-loan gains per person, and exempts from the $2.5 million income cap any operation deriving 75 percent of income from farming [S5].

Direct payments are owed every year regardless of crop prices and are tied to historical base acres and yields, so the largest landholders receive the largest checks whether or not they face hardship [S5].

The sugar program operates through nonrecourse loans and marketing allotments designed to avoid government stockpiles by supporting prices, and dairy price supports are extended at $9.90 per hundredweight through 2007 — mechanisms that raise what consumers pay for sugar and dairy products [S5].

The Senate version made it unlawful for meatpackers to own, feed, or control livestock they intend to slaughter, a provision aimed at independent livestock producers' bargaining position; that prohibition does not appear in the enacted law's livestock title, which retains only swine-contractor coverage and a right to discuss contract terms [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The nutrition, conservation, rural development, and beginning-farmer provisions deliver real, targeted help to low-income households, small towns, and new farmers [S5]. But the bill's center of gravity is Title I: guaranteed payments and price supports for commodity, sugar, dairy, and peanut producers that run through 2007 regardless of need [S5]. A bipartisan majority of the House told its conferees to adopt the Senate's tighter payment limits and bigger conservation funding, and the conference committee did not do so [S12][S5]. The result is a law that spreads genuine benefits widely while directing the largest, most secure share of new money to the biggest and most established agricultural operations, with consumers also paying more at the store for sugar and dairy.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by wide margins, a conference committee merged the House and Senate versions, both approved the final report, and the President signed it in May 2002.

narrative.text: Rep. Larry Combest introduced the bill on July 26, 2001, and the House passed it 291-120 on October 5, 2001, with 139 of 210 voting Democrats and 151 of 218 voting Republicans in favor [S9][S8].
The Senate struck the House language, substituted the text of S. 1731, and passed it 58-40 on February 13, 2002 — 48 of 50 voting Democrats yes, only 9 of 47 voting Republicans yes [S10].

On April 18, 2002 the House voted 265-158 to instruct its conferees to accept the Senate's tighter payment limitations and to seek more conservation and research funding; conferees were not bound by these instructions [S12][S8].

The conference report, filed May 1, 2002, set payment caps at $40,000 direct, $65,000 counter-cyclical, and $75,000 in marketing-loan gains per person, with a $2.5 million adjusted-gross-income test that exempts largely farm-dependent operations — looser than the Senate's limits [S5].
The House agreed to the conference report 280-141 on May 2, 2002 and the Senate 64-35 on May 8, 2002; the President signed it on May 13, 2002 as Public Law 107-171 [S16][S17][S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commodity, sugar, dairy, and peanut producers came out ahead, with guaranteed payments and price supports locked in through 2007 and the Senate's tighter payment limits set aside. Food stamp recipients, beginning farmers, and rural communities also gained real but smaller provisions.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was bipartisan — 280 House members (137 D, 141 R, 2 I) and 64 senators (43 D, 20 R, 1 I) approved the conference report — but the Senate's earlier 58-40 vote split sharply by party, with 48 of 50 voting Democrats in favor and only 9 of 49 Republicans.

industries.industry: Commodity crop producers (wheat, corn, cotton, rice, soybeans, other oilseeds)
industries.note: The bill guarantees direct payments through 2007 regardless of prices, adds counter-cyclical payments when prices fall below targets, and restores marketing loans, with caps of $40,000, $65,000, and $75,000 per person respectively [S5]. Because payments follow historical base acres, the largest operations receive the most, and the cost lands on taxpayers.

The bill extends the sugar program through 2007 with nonrecourse loans, storage-facility loans, and marketing allotments, and requires the program to run without federal cost by supporting prices [S5]. Consumers and sugar-using food makers pay the difference between supported domestic prices and world prices.

Milk price supports are extended at $9.90 per hundredweight through 2007 and a national dairy market loss payment program is created for 2002 through 2005 [S5]. The support program works by government purchases of dairy products, which holds retail milk, butter, and cheese prices up.

The marketing quota program is terminated, but quota holders are compensated at $0.11 per pound through 2006, and producers get direct payments, counter-cyclical payments, and $355-per-ton marketing loans [S5]. Taxpayers fund the buyout while ending a system that had limited who could grow peanuts.

The final law tightens some contract rules — swine contractors come under the Packers and Stockyards Act and producers gain the right to discuss contract terms with advisers — and requires humane disposal of nonambulatory livestock [S5]. But the Senate-passed ban on packer ownership of livestock, sought by independent ranchers, is absent from the enacted law [S4][S5].

The bill creates grants for biorefineries, loans and grants for on-farm renewable energy systems and energy efficiency, and requires federal agencies to purchase biobased products where price and performance are comparable [S5]. It builds a market for farm-grown energy at modest taxpayer cost.

industries.industry: Food stamp households and low-income families
industries.note: The bill raises the food stamp standard deduction to 8.31 percent of the poverty guideline, allows transitional benefits for families leaving welfare, and restores eligibility for legal immigrant children and five-year residents [S5]. These are direct gains for low-income people, though they are a modest share of the bill's total spending.
